name: Navigation Layer
description: Describes how a user moves through the application: routes and route parameters, navigation flows and their steps, guards and redirects, menus, deep links and the transitions between views (single-page-application navigation patterns). Router configuration and route tables are the usual evidence; the views reached belong to the UX layer and server-side HTTP endpoints to the API layer. Modelling rules: a navigation graph composes its routes and transitions and aggregates its flows, guards and breadcrumb configurations; a route composes its route meta and may contain child routes; a flow composes its steps and aggregates the context variables it carries. A transition leaves its source route (the route flows to it) and navigates to its destination route; a flow step navigates to its route, and a guard action redirects by navigating to a route. A guard evaluates its condition, triggers its action on denial and protects what it guards (routes, transitions, flows and flow steps); the condition and the action do not link to each other. Context variables are passive state: the steps, guards, conditions, actions and transitions that read or write them access them, and their value types map to data-model schema properties or reference data objects and schema documents. A breadcrumb configuration references the route meta it reads labels from, its home route and the flows it shows progress for. Across layers, a route maps to the UX view it renders and may lazy-load or depend on application components; routes, steps and guards use application services, access the data-model schemas they load or check, and are served by the API operations they call; they never reach the data store directly. Navigation reaches the business and motivation layers through the product user workflows and workflow steps that flows and steps realize, and satisfies requirements, constraints and principles.
